title: Sound
description: Animated KS3 Physics lesson on sound for ages 9 to 14: vibrations, sound waves, what sound travels through, amplitude and loudness, frequency and pitch, how we hear, hearing range, echoes and the speed of sound.
intro: Vibrations, sound waves, loudness and pitch, how your ears work, echoes and the speed of sound, explained by the owl in five short parts.

steps.say: All sounds are made by **vibrations**. A vibration is something moving backwards and forwards very quickly, like a plucked guitar string.
Hum and touch your throat: you can feel your **vocal cords** vibrating. A drum skin vibrates when you hit it.
The vibrating object pushes on the air particles next to it. They bump into their neighbours and pass the vibration on.
This travelling vibration is a **sound wave**. Each particle only jiggles backwards and forwards. It is the energy that travels, not the air.
The particles vibrate along the same direction that the sound travels. This is called a **longitudinal** wave.

check.q: A sound travels across a room to your ear. What do the air particles do?
options: They vibrate backwards and forwards and pass the vibration on
They travel all the way from the sound to your ear
check.hint: Think of the red particle in the picture. Did it go all the way across, or stay near the same place?
check.explain: Each particle **vibrates** backwards and forwards about the same place and bumps the next one. The vibration (and its energy) travels to your ear, not the air itself.

steps.say: Sound needs particles to pass the vibration along. It can travel through **solids**, **liquids** and **gases**. The material it travels through is called the **medium**.
A **vacuum** is completely empty space: no particles at all. So sound cannot travel through it. Pump the air out of a jar with a ringing bell inside, and the sound fades away.
Space is almost a vacuum, so it is silent. Astronauts talk to each other by radio, because radio waves can travel through empty space.
Sound is usually fastest in solids, where the particles are close together and strongly joined. It travels at about 340 m/s in air, about 1500 m/s in water and about 5000 m/s in steel.

check.q: Two astronauts on a spacewalk can't hear each other shout, even when they are close. Why?
options: Space is a vacuum, so there are no particles to carry the sound
It is too cold in space for sound
Sound travels too fast in space to hear
check.hint: What does sound need to pass the vibration along? Is there any of it in space?
check.explain: Sound is passed on by particles. Space is almost a **vacuum**, with no particles to carry it, so the shout can't reach the other astronaut.

steps.say: A microphone and a screen can show a sound as a wavy line. This lets us see what the sound is like.
The height of the wave is the **amplitude**. Bigger vibrations give a bigger amplitude and a **louder** sound.
The number of vibrations each second is the **frequency**. It is measured in **hertz** (Hz). 100 Hz means 100 vibrations every second.
steps.speak: The number of vibrations each second is the frequency. It is measured in hertz. 100 hertz means 100 vibrations every second.

steps.say: More waves squeezed onto the screen means a higher frequency, and that sounds like a higher **pitch**. A big drum has a low pitch. A whistle has a high pitch.

check.q: On the same screen, wave B is the same height as wave A, but it has more waves squeezed in. How does B sound compared with A?
check.hint: Height (amplitude) tells you about loudness. The number of waves (frequency) tells you about pitch. Which one changed?
check.explain: More waves in the same time means a higher **frequency**, so a **higher pitch**. The height is the same, so it is just as loud.

steps.say: Your outer ear collects sound and funnels it down the ear canal. The sound makes your **eardrum** vibrate.
Three tiny bones pass the vibrations on to the **cochlea**. The cochlea turns them into electrical signals, which travel along a nerve to your **brain**.
Young people can hear sounds from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. This is the **hearing range**. The top of the range gets lower as people get older.
steps.speak: Young people can hear sounds from about 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz. This is the hearing range. The top of the range gets lower as people get older.

steps.say: Sounds above 20,000 Hz are **ultrasound**: too high for us to hear, but dogs and bats can. Sounds below 20 Hz are **infrasound**. Elephants use infrasound to call to each other.
steps.speak: Sounds above 20,000 hertz are ultrasound: too high for us to hear, but dogs and bats can. Sounds below 20 hertz are infrasound. Elephants use infrasound to call to each other.

steps.say: Very loud sounds can damage the cochlea for ever. People who work with loud machines wear **ear defenders** to protect their hearing.

check.q: A bat squeaks at 50,000 Hz. Can people hear it?
options: No: it is ultrasound, above 20,000 Hz
Yes: people can hear every sound
No: it is infrasound, below 20 Hz
Only if they stand very close
check.hint: Our hearing range is about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Is 50,000 Hz inside that range, above it or below it?
check.explain: 50,000 Hz is above the top of our hearing range (20,000 Hz), so it is **ultrasound**. Being close or loud doesn't help: the pitch is simply too high for human ears.

steps.say: Sound travels at about 340 m/s in air. Light is much, much faster: about 300,000,000 m/s. So in a storm you see the lightning first and hear the thunder later.
steps.speak: Sound travels at about 340 metres per second in air. Light is much, much faster: about 300 million metres per second. So in a storm you see the lightning first and hear the thunder later.

steps.say: **Distance = speed × time**. You hear the thunder 3 s after the flash. The storm is about 340 × 3 = 1020 m away: about 1 km.
steps.speak: Distance equals speed times time. You hear the thunder 3 seconds after the flash. The storm is about 340 times 3, which is 1020 metres away: about 1 kilometre.

steps.say: Sound bounces off hard surfaces, like a cliff or a wall. A reflected sound is called an **echo**.
You shout at a cliff and hear the echo 4 s later. The sound went there and back: 340 × 4 = 1360 m. So the cliff is 1360 ÷ 2 = 680 m away.
steps.speak: You shout at a cliff and hear the echo 4 seconds later. The sound went there and back: 340 times 4 is 1360 metres. So the cliff is 1360 divided by 2, which is 680 metres away.

steps.say: Soft things like curtains and carpets **absorb** sound, so they cut down echoes. Bats send out ultrasound and listen for the echoes to find their food.

check.q: You clap near a wall and hear the echo 1 s later. Sound travels at 340 m/s. How far away is the wall?
check.hint: In 1 s the sound travels 340 m. But that is there AND back. How far is it just one way?
check.explain: 340 m/s × 1 s = 340 m there and back. Halve it: 340 ÷ 2 = **170 m** to the wall.
